question.worked_solution:
We note that $q=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $3q$ and $4q.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3q,4q)=12q.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $12q,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2q-1}{4q} & =\frac{q+1}{3q}-1 \\ 12q\cdot (\frac{2q-1}{4q}) & =12q\cdot (\frac{q+1}{3q}-1) \\ 12q\cdot \frac{2q-1}{4q} & =12q\cdot \frac{q+1}{3q}-12q\cdot 1 \\ 3\cdot \cancel{4q}\cdot (\frac{2q-1}{\cancel{4q}}) & =4\cdot \cancel{3q}\cdot (\frac{q+1}{\cancel{3q}})-12q \\ 3(2q-1) & =4(q+1)-12q\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $q,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(2q-1) & =4(q+1)-12q \\ 6q-3 & =4q+4-12q \\ 6q-3 & =-8q+4 \\ 6q+8q & =4+3 \\ 14q & =7 \\ q & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $q=0$ as a solution. But since $q=\frac{1}{2}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $q=\frac{1}{2}.$
